--- title: Documentation type: slides order: 3 author: Luisa Orozco, Barbara Vreede description: Day 3 Code Refinery --- # Documentation === === ## Examples of documentation + Think of projects with good documentation. _What do you like about them?_ + Think of projects with less good documentation. _What don't you like about them? Are you missing anything?_ NB: You can choose a mature library with lots of users, but try to also think of less mature projects you had to collaborate on, or papers you had to reproduce. === ## Types of documentation
+ README files and CITATION files + In-code documentation (Docstrings) + API documentation + Tutorials + ...
=== ## A good README file + README file is first thing a user/collaborator sees + What should be included in README files?
  • ...
  • ...
  • ...
  • ...
  • ...
  • ...
  • ...
Note: + A descriptive project title + Motivation (why the project exists) and basics + Installation / How to setup + Copy-pasteable quick start code example + Usage reference (if not elsewhere) + Citation if someone uses it + Other related tools ("see also") + Contact information for the developer(s) + Badges + License information + Contributing guidelines === ## Badges Badges are a way to quickly show the status of a project: is it building, is it tested, what is the license? You typically find them on top of the README file. ![Badges on top of a Readme file](media/documentation/documentation-badges.png). === ## Why citation? + Unlike papers, softwares are difficult to cite + To get credit, provide citation information at the root of your project, e.g. using a CITATION.cff (Citation File Format) file. + Citation files are easy to create (e.g. using cffinit) + Gather all the required information in one place + Automatically picked up by platforms like GitHub, Zenodo ... === ## Minimal example of CITATION.cff file ```yaml authors: - family-names: Doe given-names: Jane cff-version: 1.2.0 message: "If you use this software, please cite it using the metadata from this file." title: "My research software" ``` === ## Why write in-code documentation? In-code documentation: + Makes code more understandable + Explains decisions we made === ## When **not** to use in-code documentation? + When the code is self-explanatory + To replace good variable/function names + To replace version control + To keep old (zombie) code around === ## Readable code vs commented code ```python= # convert from degrees celsius to fahrenheit def convert(d): return d * 5 / 9 + 32 ``` vs ```python= def celsius_to_fahrenheit(degrees): return degrees * 5 / 9 + 32 ``` === ## What makes a good comment? **Comment A** 

# Now we check if temperature is larger than -50:
if temperature > -50:
    print('do something')
**Comment B** 

# We regard temperatures below -50 degrees as measurement errors
if temperature > -50:
    print('do something')
How are these different? Which one do you prefer? === ## Docstrings: a special kind of comment ```python= def celsius_to_fahrenheit(degrees): """Convert degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit.""" return degrees * 5 / 9 + 32 ``` Why is this OK? Note: Docstrings can be used to generate user documentation. They are accessible outside the code. They follow a standardized syntax. === ## In-code commenting: key points + Explicit, descriptive naming already provides important documentation. + Comments should describe the why for your code, not the what. + Writing docstrings is an easy way to write documentation while you code, as they are accessible outside the code itself. === ## User/API documentation + What if a README file is not enough? + How do I easily create user documentation? === ## Tools + Documentation generators (e.g. **mkdocs**, **Sphinx**) - creates nicely-formatted HTML pages out of .md or .rst files - numerous plugins available to extend functionality (API, spellcheck, etc.) - programming language independent - easy to use and deploy (e.g. GitHub pages) - **mkdocs** easier to start with, but **Sphinx** is more complete and robust + **Github pages** (deploy your documentation) - set up inside your GitHub repository - automatically deploys your Sphinx-generated documentation === ## Using **mkdocs** + In a new code directory, run `mkdocs new .` + Edit the `mkdocs.yml` file to configure your documentation + Run `mkdocs build` to generate the documentation site + Run `mkdocs serve` to serve the documentation site (open in your browser) + Use the `mkdocstrings` to automatically generate API documentation + Use `mkdocs gh-deploy` to deploy your documentation to GitHub === ## Using **mkdocs** ![mkdocs](media/documentation/mkdocs.png) === ## Take-home message + Depending on the purpose and state of the project documentation needs to meet different criteria. + Documentation can take different shapes: + Readable code + In-code comments + Docstrings + README files + Tutorials/notebooks + Documentation is a vital part of a project, and should be kept and created alongside the corresponding code.

contents.plainText:
--- title: Modular Code type: slides order: 2 author: Barbara Vreede, Ole Mussmann description: Modular coding --- # Developing Modular Code === ## What is modularity? Simple components combined to produce complex behavior. - Software can be 'built up' from smaller elements. - Elements are self-contained and independent. - Each element handles a specific (set of) task(s). === ## Modular code
=== ## What are these blocks/elements?
  • functions
  • classes
  • modules
  • libraries/packages
  • programs
  • ...
=== ## Why write modular code? To increase robustness - A well-designed module can be tested. - This helps keep the codebase well-functioning and bug-free. === ## Why write modular code? To make maintenance easier: - Modular code is more readable and understandable. - Modules can be debugged separately. - Modules only need to be improved/optimized once. === ## Why write modular code? To allow reusability: - A module can live independent of its original context. - It can be reused by another project. === ## Why write modular code? To facilitate scalability:
  • Complexity remains low by design.
  • This creates space for scaling up.
=== ## Why write modular code? To create opportunities for innovation: - Modules increase the capabilities and power of a project. - Rearrange old modules for new applications. === ## Why write modular code? To save time: === ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
=== ## Naming your module - be descriptive and clear - focus on human intelligibility - follow language specific conventions - avoid abbreviations
=== ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
  • is readable
=== ## More readable != shorter code Shorter: ```python indexATG = [n for n,i in enumerate(myList) if i == 'ATG'] indexAAG = [n for n,i in enumerate(myList) if i == 'AAG'] ``` More modular: ```python def getIndex(inputList,z): zIndex = [n for n,i in enumerate(inputList) if i == z] return zIndex indexATG = getIndex(myList,'ATG') indexAAG = getIndex(myList,'AAG') ``` === ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
  • is readable
  • is pure and predictable
=== ## An impure function... ... does not always give the same result: ```python def fahrenheit_to_celsius(temp_list, converted_temps=[]): for temp in temp_list: temp_c = (temp - 32.0) * (5.0/9.0) converted_temps.append(temp_c) return converted_temps >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0] ``` **Q: What will happen when we call the function a second time?** ```python >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0, 0.0, 25.0] ``` === ## A pure function... ... always gives the same result: ```python def fahrenheit_to_celsius(temp_list, converted_temps=None): if converted_temps == None: converted_temps = [] for temp in temp_list: temp_c = (temp - 32.0) * (5.0/9.0) converted_temps.append(temp_c) return converted_temps >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0] >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0] ``` === ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
  • is readable
  • is pure and predictable
=== ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
=== ## Readable code Modular code becomes more readable - Code is read more than it is written - Does a reader understand what the code does? - Bad readability can be a "code smell" === ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
  • repetition
=== ## Repetitive code - Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY): place reused code into a function - Identify functions units by their _action_ - (e.g. "plot", "transform", "extract", "save")
=== ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
  • repetition
  • nested code
=== ## Target nested code Nested code is a prime target for modularization: ```python def sum_even_numbers(bottom, top): if top > bottom: sum = 0 for x in range(bottom, top): if x % 2 == 0: sum += x return sum return 0 sum_even_numbers(2, 14) # 42 ``` === ## Reduce nestedness... ... by extracting modules: ```python def _filter_even(number): if number % 2 == 0: return number return 0 def sum_even_numbers(bottom, top): if top < bottom: return 0 sum = 0 for x in range(bottom, top): sum += _filter_even(x) return sum sum_even_numbers (2,14) # 42 ``` === ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
  • repetition
  • nested code
=== ## Let tests help you - Write tests for each individual module - Use the test-writing procedure to look critically at the module's function: - Is the input/output clear? - What can you not yet test? Extract it into a new module.

Everyone is used to testing their software in one way or another. The simplest way is manual interactive testing, where you call your function manually in, for example, a Jupyter notebook and check the output is what you expect.

Besides, constantly doing the same thing in order to perform manual tests sounds an awful lot like something we can automate right? That's exactly what automated testing is: writing functions to perform the testing you would otherwise do manually. The obvious benefit being that once you have these tests, the computer can automatically run them all for you.

Once you've started with tests, or unit tests specifically, you'll probably notice a similar thing happening as in your regular code: repetitions.
Testing a certain function for different cases can of course be done by repeating the same test code with different values. In your 'normal' code, you would solve this with for-loops. This will still work in tests too, but then each case would not be shown as a separate test.
Pytest has a solution for this: parametrization. You'll learn how you can still specify your test to work on a single case at a time, and then specify the different cases above it. Pytest then takes care of running each of them.

The goal of having different cases is to make sure that all possible ways your code can run are checked. In testing terms, this is usually refered to as coverage. By running your tests with coverage, it'll let you know which lines are or aren't covered. This is a great way to check if you're forgetting to test any cases your code can handle, or to help decide what tests to write next.
Don't get distracted by the percentage coverage number though. It's very easy to write tests to get 100% test coverage, without actually testing anything of your code. As with anything: a metric can quickly stop being helpful when you use it as a goal.

When you've written your tests, it would of course be best to have your tests run automatically too. When working with GitHub as your remote repository, you can configure GitHub to automatically run all tests when new commits are pushed to a branch, or on other triggers. This means you'll automatically get feedback on your code, even if you forgot to run the tests on your own machine before pushing the changes. This functionality is called 'GitHub Actions', and GitHub very kindly allows every project some free minutes of runtime at this.

Finally in this episode, you'll have a look at PyCharm's debug mode. It's a different way of running your code in PyCharm that's a bit slower, but will let you interrupt your program using preset break points so you can step through your code one instruction at a time. When stepping through code, PyCharm will let you look at the current values of all variables that exist in your program, and tells you exactly which functions were called to get to where you currently are.
This not only works when you've manually set break points, but also when your code runs into an exception on its own. Both ways are great tools to track down bugs and to determine how to fix them.
Remember that when you've found (and fixed) a bug, that those situations make excellent test cases, usually referred to as 'Regression tests'. By writing tests of the situations that could be used to recreate bugs you've encountered and fixed, you'll guarantee that the same bug shouldn't pop up again. Or at least not undetected!

Wouldn't it make sense to not throw that value away?
Amount of reuse is hard to predict

A lot of widely used software started out as someone's personal project. While most quick scripts won't grow into the next numpy or pandas, if your software proves useful to others, the amount and breadth of users may well grow over time.
Do you think such growth is more or less likely if the code is hard to reuse?

The best time to plant a tree is 20 years ago. The second best time is now.
Writes software to fulfill research goals (ideally from a design)
to understanding, designing, building, releasing, and maintaining software

children.value: Software designed deliberately will be much easier to work with in the long term than software we build without a plan - time spent planning in advance will save you a lot more time later.

The terms programming (or even coding) and software engineering are often used interchangeably. They are not. Someone who is engineering software takes a wider view:
The lifecycle of software: from understanding what is needed, to writing the software and using/releasing it, to what happens afterwards.
Who will (or may) be involved: software is written for stakeholders. This may only be the researcher initially, but there is an understanding that others may become involved later (even if that isn’t evident yet). A good rule of thumb is to always assume that code will be read and used by others later on, which includes yourself!
Software (or code) is an asset: software inherently contains value - for example, in terms of what it can do, the lessons learned throughout its development, and as an implementation of a research approach (i.e. a particular research algorithm, process, or technical approach).
As an asset, it could be reused: again, it may not be evident initially that the software will have use beyond its initial purpose or project, but there is an assumption that the software - or even just a part of it - could be reused in the future.

The software development process consists of multiple stages, which in the 'traditional (/ old fashioned)' waterfall model follows one step after another.
So far, you are all familiar with the "Implementation" step, as that 'simply' consists of the programming you're already doing, and you have worked a bit on the "testing" step too, to make sure what you've implemented is actually correct.
But it's also important to consider what you actually want to implement in the first place

After all, it doesn't make sense to start programming if you haven't thought about what you're going to build in the first place.
But there's more you can take into account when designing your program than just how to implement and test it.

How you deploy and eventually have/want to maintain your project can also influence your design decisions.
Although Deployment and Maintenance are typically much less 'formal' in a research (and especially in an academic) setting compared to a corporate setting.
Think of the different in running your analysis for a paper compared to deploying a new version of the ns.nl website.
 
There is actually one more step in the process.
Just like you can't build without a design, you can't really design without knowing what you want.

That's where properly specifying your requirements comes in.
Taking dedicated time to think about what the requirements of your project are can be vital in making the right (design) decisions at the start.
After all, the sooner you can correct or avoid a mistake, the cheaper it is.
Write them down so you only build what's actually needed!
What goal am I trying to achieve?
What feature do I need do achieve this?

For the first episode of this section, we'll focus on the requirements step. To really think about them, and give yourself the best chance of sticking to them later, it's best to actually write down your requirements.

This will probably feel like a lot of overhead, so will take some discipline. But by writing it down, you're forcing yourself to be specific, which helps to identify problems as soon as possible, saving you a lot of time later in the process.
When thinking about requirements of code, we should avoid the temptation to immediately think in terms of code, but instead start at a high level.
First make sure you identify what goal you're actually trying to achieve. Again, we don't want to build anything we're never going to need.
When the goal is clear, we can refine it down to start defining features the software should have...
… which can be further specified by implementation details.

These three levels can be named 'business', 'user, and 'solution', requirements. Although as the lesson materials mention, this naming scheme is actually quite arbitrary, and you may find different terminology being used in different contexts.
For this episode, talk through the exercises as a group.
How do users interact with the software?
How to solve the core research/business problem?
Now we have (some version of) the requirements in place, the next step is designing before we can get to implementation.

Software can be designed at very different levels. Just like buildings, where an architect designs the overall shape in collaboration with engineers to make sure the available materials can actually support it, all the way down to an interior designer who lays out the exact details of which pieces of furniture go where.
You can consider many aspects of design, but here are three common ones:

Architecture is the high-level design. Which (large) components does your software currently consist of, which ones will have to be added, changed or removed? And not just considering your own software, but also the wider system around it: which other software does your software interact with? Web APIs are commonly a part of this.

Think back to the "Model-View-Controller" architecture you encountered earlier. It's a way of splitting up the responsibilities of your program into separate components so we can think about their interaction at a higher level. This can be helpful, but will have its limits. No separation will ever be perfect, and certain functionality can be argued to be part of different components in the same software. There's a lot of examples with specific terminology that you can choose from if you want. It's good to be aware of common patterns: they usually appeared after many hard lessons have been learned. But don't feel to stuck by them, it should
your efforts in creating the code, not hold you back.
The User Interface or User eXperience is also subject to design. Think about clunky apps or websites, or completely losing track of how to do things when software you use frequently (
) decides to change things? If there is a preferred order of things, make sure that's easy for your users! They don't have to follow the structure of your code when interacting.

Now we're almost getting to the meat of things: which algorithms and data structures will we actually use to solve the problem we identified in the requirements? Don't forget your (non-)functional user requirements here. The space-time trade-off is commonly made here depending on your restrictions: should it be fast and do you have the space to pre-compute and memorize, or is your memory limited and is a bit of extra time not a problem?
Again, these are just common examples of what to think of when designing.
… is readable, understandable, covered by automated tests, not over complicated and does well what is intended to do
The point of spending all this time designing our code, is to make sure we produce "good code" in the end. The following quote sums it up quite nicely:

Readability and understandability goes all the way from using sensible variable names, to how you've chosen to construct your software in terms of components. The logic should be easy to see, and should make sense when explained.

Having code be testable / tested means you have some guarantee that it actually does what it's supposed to do, and also means the behavior of your components is defined well enough that you can check it.
. In short: that you won't dread having to go back to your code in a few months time if you have to find and fix a bug, or extend it to support new functionality.

Okay, so now we've covered what aspects go into designing software, and what you should pay attention to when doing so. So when we do decide we've designed enough? When are we done with preparing, and can we actually start coding?!
There is no fixed answer here, it's all a balancing act you will have to experience for yourself
The whole point of designing is not to under-design, we want to avoid technical debt!

For those unfamiliar with the term "technical debt": it is basically a shorthand for work that has to be done on refactoring/redesigning code before it becomes possible to expand it with new features. It's usually caused by under-designing and rushing implementations, choosing quick fixes over steady improvements.
It's referred to as 'debt' because by choosing those quick fixes, you're effectively "borrowing" time from the future with interest: by not spending the time designing now, you can get your feature out faster, but that lack of design will come back for you later, when it's even harder to fix because more stuff has been added, and you need extra time to get re-acquainted with the context.

You could compare it to choosing not to do the dishes right after dinner, but doing it the next day instead: You gain the free time now, but tomorrow you still have to do it, and now it's all gotten stuck and is even harder to clean.

The flip-side is over-designing: in the extreme case, you'd just keep designing and never get to coding, which isn't the point either. At least, the more important, larger, or more long-lived your software will be, the more time it makes sense to spend on designing. After all, the point of designing is to prevent mistakes. In small or short-lived software, there's a lot less that
even go wrong, than in a larger project.
Details of ‘how’ something works are hidden. You only deal with ‘what’ the code does.
You (or a user of your code) only need to understand the higher level of abstraction and not the details.
Breaking up software in smaller components to reduce the interdependence.
A change in one component does not necessitate a change in the other.
Packing data and functions operating on it in a single component.
In Python you can group together data and methods in a class. An instance of a class is called an object.
Having multiple implementations/shapes of the same abstract concept
When writing tests for some functionality, you want to depend on as little other functionality
is an object for which you define just enough behavior so it can take the place of a different object in your tests
Improving the structure of the code, without altering its function.
How can we ensure that the code still works after refactoring?

Inevitably, at some point you'll encounter code that is not designed as you'd want it to.
Whether not deliberately designed in the first place, or the latest requirements just no longer matching the previous design. That's just a natural part of iterative software development.

Refactoring is the process of redesigning existing code. If done at the same time as adding new functionality, any newly introduced bugs will be very hard to solve. Instead, it's easier to keep the functionality constant first, and then add the new feature later.

Wanting to keep the functionality constant, how do we ensure this is the case after our refactor? If you think back to the previous section, we've already discussed the ideal tool for this: tests! If our code is well tested, any change in functionality should fail at least one test. So if we redesigned the code and our tests still pass, we can be fairly sure that it still works just like before. Except now it will be easier to add the new feature we were considering.
Pure functions are easy to read, write, test and maintain, because they have no
Need to change something? Return a changed copy!
Here is an example of an impure function in use: We have two functions

that calculate the price of buying products from a shopping list at their stores.
Kruidvat sells tea and paracetamol, but does not sell cheese or pasta, so we will have to buy those products at Albert Heijn using the second function.
These functions work just like how you would use a shopping list in person: once you've bought a product, that product is crossed out or removed from your list.

As you can see, the tea and paracetamol have now been removed from the shopping list.
This means that when using the same

variable, we only end up buying cheese and pasta at Albert Heijn instead of the full list.
In this case that is the intended behavior of the programmer, but it does make the function harder to use generically, harder to document and harder to test.
For example, we can't easily re-use the same shopping list to check which order of shopping would be cheaper: our shopping list is empty after calling both for the first time, and in this case we don't have a copy of the original anymore.

In short, a pure function should always return the same output for the same input, and should not change anything outside itself.
This also means it should be independent of any other local/global variables that may be around.
By writing our functions this way, they usually become easier to work with, and especially to test: there will never be any (unexpected) dependencies on other tests or state.

How might we rewrite this to be pure functions?
One way could be to first create a function that returns a new list with only those items available at that store

With these new functions, our original shopping list is unchanged.
We could then write separate functions that calculate the price for certain items at a certain store.
Those can then be combined in another function that takes care of buying things from the shopping list in order so we don't buy anything twice.
Note that this is just an example/suggestion, and other/better ways of structuring functionality might be possible

the original implementation, while it might be a bit more work to separate out the functions like this, we do end up with functions that are smaller, do a single clear thing and are much easier to test.
The concept of only programming with such pure functions is a paradigm called

, and is one of several programming paradigms that Python supports.
(Other paradigms can include procedural and object oriented programming)

Think of the different in running your analysis for a paper compared to deploying a new version of the ns.nl website.   There is actually one more step in the process. Just like you can't build without a design, you can't really design without knowing what you want.   *point out 'Requirement Gather & Analysis'*   That's where properly specifying your requirements comes in. Taking dedicated time to think about what the requirements of your project are can be vital in making the right (design) decisions at the start. After all, the sooner you can correct or avoid a mistake, the cheaper it is. ==

Software development as a continuous process

Requirements will almost always change on reflection!
== Note: Image from: https://blog.stackademic.com/understanding-lean-startup-and-agile-development-c42677a95d03 === ## 3.1 Software Requirements Write them down so you only build what's actually needed!
  • Start high level
    • What goal am I trying to achieve?

  • Refine
    • What feature do I need do achieve this?

  • Make specific
    • How do I implement that?
Note: For the first episode of this section, we'll focus on the requirements step. To really think about them, and give yourself the best chance of sticking to them later, it's best to actually write down your requirements. This will probably feel like a lot of overhead, so will take some discipline. But by writing it down, you're forcing yourself to be specific, which helps to identify problems as soon as possible, saving you a lot of time later in the process. When thinking about requirements of code, we should avoid the temptation to immediately think in terms of code, but instead start at a high level. ** reveal 'Start high level' ** First make sure you identify what goal you're actually trying to achieve. Again, we don't want to build anything we're never going to need. ** reveal 'Refine' ** When the goal is clear, we can refine it down to start defining features the software should have... ** reveal 'Make specific' ** … which can be further specified by implementation details. These three levels can be named 'business', 'user, and 'solution', requirements. Although as the lesson materials mention, this naming scheme is actually quite arbitrary, and you may find different terminology being used in different contexts. >> For this episode, talk through the exercises as a group. === ## 3.2 Software Architecture and Design
  • Software/System Architecture
    • How do components interact?

  • UI/UX
    • How do users interact with the software?

  • Algorithm Design
    • How to solve the core research/business problem?
Note: Now we have (some version of) the requirements in place, the next step is designing before we can get to implementation. Software can be designed at very different levels. Just like buildings, where an architect designs the overall shape in collaboration with engineers to make sure the available materials can actually support it, all the way down to an interior designer who lays out the exact details of which pieces of furniture go where. You can consider many aspects of design, but here are three common ones: ** reveal Architecture ** Architecture is the high-level design. Which (large) components does your software currently consist of, which ones will have to be added, changed or removed? And not just considering your own software, but also the wider system around it: which other software does your software interact with? Web APIs are commonly a part of this. Think back to the "Model-View-Controller" architecture you encountered earlier. It's a way of splitting up the responsibilities of your program into separate components so we can think about their interaction at a higher level. This can be helpful, but will have its limits. No separation will ever be perfect, and certain functionality can be argued to be part of different components in the same software. There's a lot of examples with specific terminology that you can choose from if you want. It's good to be aware of common patterns: they usually appeared after many hard lessons have been learned. But don't feel to stuck by them, it should **help** your efforts in creating the code, not hold you back. ** reveal UI/UX ** The User Interface or User eXperience is also subject to design. Think about clunky apps or websites, or completely losing track of how to do things when software you use frequently ( *cough* MS Teams *cough*) decides to change things? If there is a preferred order of things, make sure that's easy for your users! They don't have to follow the structure of your code when interacting. ** reveal Algorithm Design ** Now we're almost getting to the meat of things: which algorithms and data structures will we actually use to solve the problem we identified in the requirements? Don't forget your (non-)functional user requirements here. The space-time trade-off is commonly made here depending on your restrictions: should it be fast and do you have the space to pre-compute and memorize, or is your memory limited and is a bit of extra time not a problem? Again, these are just common examples of what to think of when designing. == ## Good Code
… is readable, understandable, covered by automated tests, not over complicated and does well what is intended to do

— Intent HQ blog

Note: blog: https://intenthq.com/writing/what-is-good-code-a-scientific-definition The point of spending all this time designing our code, is to make sure we produce "good code" in the end. The following quote sums it up quite nicely: ** click to reveal quote ** Readability and understandability goes all the way from using sensible variable names, to how you've chosen to construct your software in terms of components. The logic should be easy to see, and should make sense when explained. Having code be testable / tested means you have some guarantee that it actually does what it's supposed to do, and also means the behavior of your components is defined well enough that you can check it. Together, this makes code **maintainable**. In short: that you won't dread having to go back to your code in a few months time if you have to find and fix a bug, or extend it to support new functionality. == ## Finding balance
- Under-design - Technical Debt
- Over-design - Overhead
Note: Okay, so now we've covered what aspects go into designing software, and what you should pay attention to when doing so. So when we do decide we've designed enough? When are we done with preparing, and can we actually start coding?! ** click to reveal image ** There is no fixed answer here, it's all a balancing act you will have to experience for yourself ** click to reveal under-design/tech debt ** The whole point of designing is not to under-design, we want to avoid technical debt! For those unfamiliar with the term "technical debt": it is basically a shorthand for work that has to be done on refactoring/redesigning code before it becomes possible to expand it with new features. It's usually caused by under-designing and rushing implementations, choosing quick fixes over steady improvements. It's referred to as 'debt' because by choosing those quick fixes, you're effectively "borrowing" time from the future with interest: by not spending the time designing now, you can get your feature out faster, but that lack of design will come back for you later, when it's even harder to fix because more stuff has been added, and you need extra time to get re-acquainted with the context. You could compare it to choosing not to do the dishes right after dinner, but doing it the next day instead: You gain the free time now, but tomorrow you still have to do it, and now it's all gotten stuck and is even harder to clean. ** click to reveal over-design ** The flip-side is over-designing: in the extreme case, you'd just keep designing and never get to coding, which isn't the point either. At least, the more important, larger, or more long-lived your software will be, the more time it makes sense to spend on designing. After all, the point of designing is to prevent mistakes. In small or short-lived software, there's a lot less that **can** even go wrong, than in a larger project. === ## 6 Techniques for Good Software Design Episode 3.3 - Code Abstraction - Code Decoupling - Encapsulation - Polymorphism Episode 3.4 - Code Refactoring - Pure Functions === ## 3.3 Code Abstraction
Details of ‘how’ something works are hidden. You only deal with ‘what’ the code does. You (or a user of your code) only need to understand the higher level of abstraction and not the details.
== ## 3.3 Code Decoupling
Breaking up software in smaller components to reduce the interdependence. A change in one component does not necessitate a change in the other. Clear interface between components
== ## 3.3 Encapsulation
Packing data and functions operating on it in a single component. In Python you can group together data and methods in a class. An instance of a class is called an object.
== ## 3.3 Polymorphism
Having multiple implementations/shapes of the same abstract concept
== ## 3.3 Testing with Mocks - When writing tests for some functionality, you want to depend on as little other functionality - A _mock_ is an object for which you define just enough behavior so it can take the place of a different object in your tests Sounds familiar? - Concept has been encapsulated - Implementation has been abstracted === ## 3.4 Code Refactoring Improving the structure of the code, without altering its function. How can we ensure that the code still works after refactoring? Note: Inevitably, at some point you'll encounter code that is not designed as you'd want it to. Whether not deliberately designed in the first place, or the latest requirements just no longer matching the previous design. That's just a natural part of iterative software development. Refactoring is the process of redesigning existing code. If done at the same time as adding new functionality, any newly introduced bugs will be very hard to solve. Instead, it's easier to keep the functionality constant first, and then add the new feature later. Wanting to keep the functionality constant, how do we ensure this is the case after our refactor? If you think back to the previous section, we've already discussed the ideal tool for this: tests! If our code is well tested, any change in functionality should fail at least one test. So if we redesigned the code and our tests still pass, we can be fairly sure that it still works just like before. Except now it will be easier to add the new feature we were considering. == ## 3.4 Pure vs Impure functions Pure functions are easy to read, write, test and maintain, because they have no _side effects_: - Perform an action - Leave input unchanged Need to change something? Return a changed copy! == ## Example: Impure functions Note: Here is an example of an impure function in use: We have two functions `shop_at_Albert_Heijn` and `shop_at_Kruidvat` that calculate the price of buying products from a shopping list at their stores. Kruidvat sells tea and paracetamol, but does not sell cheese or pasta, so we will have to buy those products at Albert Heijn using the second function. These functions work just like how you would use a shopping list in person: once you've bought a product, that product is crossed out or removed from your list. == ## Example: Impure functions Note: As you can see, the tea and paracetamol have now been removed from the shopping list. This means that when using the same `shopping_list` variable, we only end up buying cheese and pasta at Albert Heijn instead of the full list. In this case that is the intended behavior of the programmer, but it does make the function harder to use generically, harder to document and harder to test. For example, we can't easily re-use the same shopping list to check which order of shopping would be cheaper: our shopping list is empty after calling both for the first time, and in this case we don't have a copy of the original anymore. In short, a pure function should always return the same output for the same input, and should not change anything outside itself. This also means it should be independent of any other local/global variables that may be around. By writing our functions this way, they usually become easier to work with, and especially to test: there will never be any (unexpected) dependencies on other tests or state. == ## Example: Pure functions Note: How might we rewrite this to be pure functions? One way could be to first create a function that returns a new list with only those items available at that store == ## Example: Pure functions Note: With these new functions, our original shopping list is unchanged. We could then write separate functions that calculate the price for certain items at a certain store. Those can then be combined in another function that takes care of buying things from the shopping list in order so we don't buy anything twice. Note that this is just an example/suggestion, and other/better ways of structuring functionality might be possible However we end up **refactoring** the original implementation, while it might be a bit more work to separate out the functions like this, we do end up with functions that are smaller, do a single clear thing and are much easier to test. The concept of only programming with such pure functions is a paradigm called _functional programming_, and is one of several programming paradigms that Python supports. (Other paradigms can include procedural and object oriented programming) ===

# Digital Skills Slides
This repository holds the slide decks for lessons in the digital skills curriculum of the Netherlands eScience Center. It is built using the [NEBULA framework](https://github.com/esciencecenter-digital-skills/NEBULA).

For elaborate setup instructions and other documentation, see the [NEBULA documentation](https://github.com/esciencecenter-digital-skills/NEBULA-docs)


## Quick local setup

More detailed information about local setup can be found in the [NEBULA local rendering docs](https://github.com/esciencecenter-digital-skills/NEBULA-docs/blob/main/local-rendering.md)

### Content directory/repository

To use NEBULA to build the content in this repository locally, you will need to clone this repository and the NEBULA repository:

```bash
git clone git@github.com:esciencecenter-digital-skills/digital-skills-slides.git
git clone git@github.com:esciencecenter-digital-skills/NEBULA.git
```

### Link to the content repository

To make sure that NEBULA knows where to find the content, we create the following environment variable:

```bash
export CONTENT_PATH="path/to/your/content/repository"
```

NOTE: You cannot use a ~ in your path, you have to provide the absolute path as returned with `pwd`.

### Install dependencies
First move into the NEBULA folder (so not the content folder):
```bash
cd NEBULA
```

Install the dependencies using the [node package manager](https://docs.npmjs.com/downloading-and-installing-node-js-and-npm):

```bash
# node package manager
npm install
```

### Local development build

Start the development server on `http://localhost:3000`:

```bash
# node package manager
npm run dev
```

Now you can open a browser and navigate to `http://localhost:3000/digital-skills-slides`
